claims.claim: Presidential signing statements are a real instrument with real institutional consequences
claims.sourceSpan: Presidential signing statements are official pronouncements issued by the President contemporaneously to the signing of a bill into law

claims.claim: APP definition of a signing statement, verbatim
claims.sourceSpan: A “Signing Statement” is a written comment issued by a President at the time of signing legislation.

claims.claim: CRS definition of signing statements, verbatim and complete
claims.sourceSpan: official pronouncements issued by the President contemporaneously to the signing of a bill into law that, in addition to commenting on the law generally, have been used to forward the President's interpretation of the statutory language; to assert constitutional objections to the provisions contained therein; and, concordantly, to announce that the provisions of the law will be administered in a manner that comports with the administration's conception of the President's constitutional prerogatives

claims.claim: No constitutional provision authorises signing statements - now quoted as the full source sentence, with the source's own capital T
claims.sourceSpan: There is no explicit constitutional provision authorizing the issuance of presidential signing statements.

claims.claim: CONFIRMED MISQUOTE of a named organisation. The article attributed to the ABA the words "contrary to the rule of law and our constitutional system." notes:
First-refresh audit of a May 2026 pre-lane explainer, Phase B session 7 (veto cluster). This one was a rewrite, not an edit: the sweep called it a rewrite candidate and it was right.

THE PAGE MISQUOTED A NAMED ORGANISATION AND ITS OWN CITED AUTHORITY REBUTTED ITS HEADLINE NUMBER. Both confirmed independently before anything was changed.

First, the ABA. The article attributed to the American Bar Association the words 'contrary to the rule of law and our constitutional system'. The report says 'contrary to the rule of law and our constitutional separation of powers', and says it only of statements that 'claim the authority or state the intention to disregard or decline to enforce all or part of a law ... or to interpret such a law in a manner inconsistent with the clear intent of Congress'. The article altered the words and dropped the condition, which is what turns a bounded objection into a blanket one. The body was also misnamed: it was the ABA's Task Force on Presidential Signing Statements and the Separation of Powers Doctrine, August 2006. CORRECTIONS-BORDERLINE, FLAGGED FOR JAMES, NOT LOGGED, per handoff SS9.1 D1.

Second, the Bush count. The article published 'signing statements challenging over 1,200 specific statutory provisions - more than all previous presidents combined'. CRS RL33667 says 'more than 1,000', twice; the string 1,200 appears nowhere in it. And there is no prior-president provisions total in any source to compare against, so the second half cannot be checked at all - while on the metric that IS comparable, Bush is third of four: Reagan 250 statements, Clinton 381, G.H.W. Bush 228, G.W. Bush 161. The American Presidency Project page the article itself cited answers the question in terms: 'No, Bill Clinton issued many more signing statements. The controversy was about the kind of signing statements Bush issued.' The real story - density, not volume - is now the page's story, with the two best-known Bush statements quoted.

Third, and live on an indexed page: the meta description promised 'why courts take them seriously' and the og description said they 'carry legal weight', while the body said the opposite in two sentences. Both rewritten.

Fourth: 'Presidential signing statements are published in the Federal Register' was wrong in the body, in the Key Sources box, in the JSON-LD citation array and in a live outbound link. RL33667's only Federal Register mention in this connection is an unenacted 2009 bill that WOULD have required publication there. GovInfo names the actual venue and lists 'Statements regarding bill signings and vetoes' among its contents.

ALSO REMOVED, not softened: the whole rhetorical/interpretive/constitutional taxonomy that structured a third of the article (RL33667 uses no such scheme - 'rhetorical' returns zero hits); the claim that courts weigh signing statements against 'the legislative history in the Congressional Record' (the phrase Congressional Record appears nowhere in the report, and the framing is far more favourable than the source); an OLC standing-institutional-role claim; 'Senate hearings' (the word hearing appears zero times); 'relatively obscure until the George W. Bush administration' (the report records the practice from Monroe, an 1830 controversy, statements as common instruments by 1950, and Supreme Court citations in 1983 and 1986); 'now standard practice' (which the report's own account of the Obama decline cuts against); the signing-ceremony framing; and the attribution to Bush of inspector-general reporting objections, which in RL33667 are Obama's.

CONVERGENCE: three rounds.
